questions.scenario: A statement endpoint accepts ?sort=value_date and builds "... ORDER BY " + sort into a native query. A tester sends sort=(SELECT pg_sleep(10)) and the request takes ten seconds.
questions.question: What is the correct fix?
options: Map allowed sort names to known column names with an allow-list and reject anything else
Catch the timeout and retry
Pass sort as a bind parameter in the ORDER BY clause
Escape single quotes in the sort value
questions.explanation: Identifiers such as column names cannot be bind parameters, and escaping is not a reliable defence. An allow-list maps user choices to safe, fixed identifiers.

questions.scenario: A merchant portal lets merchants set a 'logo URL' that the server downloads and resizes. A tester sets it to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ and receives cloud credentials in the error message.
questions.question: What class of vulnerability is this?
options: Clickjacking
Cross-site scripting
Cross-site request forgery
Server-side request forgery (SSRF)
questions.explanation: The server was made to request an internal address on the attacker's behalf. Allow-lists, blocking private and link-local ranges after DNS resolution, and IMDSv2 are the defences.

questions.scenario: A production Spring Boot service exposes management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=* on its public port.
questions.question: Which endpoint is most dangerous to leave exposed?
options: /actuator/prometheus
/actuator/info
/actuator/health
/actuator/heapdump, which can contain secrets, tokens and customer data from memory
questions.explanation: A heap dump is a copy of the JVM's memory, including credentials and personal data. Expose only what you need, on a protected port.

questions.scenario: The OTP verification endpoint for transfers accepts unlimited attempts on a 6-digit code that is valid for 10 minutes.
questions.question: Which OWASP risk does this design flaw represent, and what control fixes it?
options: Insecure design / authentication failure: limit attempts per OTP and per user, shorten validity and alert on spikes
Cryptographic failure: encrypt the OTP in transit
Injection: use parameterised queries
Security misconfiguration: hide the endpoint from Swagger UI
questions.explanation: One million combinations can be tried quickly without limits. Attempt limits, short expiry and monitoring make brute force impractical.

questions.scenario: You are reviewing what a payments service writes to its logs.
questions.question: Which items must never be logged in full? (Choose two.)
options: The HTTP status code returned
The trace ID of the request
Access and refresh tokens
Card numbers (PAN) and CVV
questions.explanation: Card data and tokens give attackers direct value if logs leak, and PCI DSS forbids storing CVV. Trace IDs and status codes are safe and useful.

questions.scenario: An integration parses ISO 20022 XML payment messages from a partner using DocumentBuilderFactory with default settings.
questions.question: What should be configured?
options: Convert XML to JSON with string replacement first
Increase the parser's memory limit
Nothing: XML from partners is trusted
Disable DOCTYPE declarations and external entities to prevent XXE
questions.explanation: Default Java XML parsers can resolve external entities, letting crafted documents read files or make internal requests. Disallowing DOCTYPEs closes XXE.

questions.scenario: A message-queue consumer reads payloads with ObjectInputStream.readObject() from a topic that partner systems can publish to.
questions.question: What is the risk and the better approach?
options: The only risk is slower performance
There is no risk because the topic is internal
The risk is solved by compressing the payload
Insecure deserialisation can lead to remote code execution; use JSON mapped to explicit DTOs (or at minimum a strict serialisation filter)
questions.explanation: Java native deserialisation of untrusted data can instantiate gadget chains that run code. Data-only formats with explicit types remove that capability.
